item.title: Jamaat ameer congratulates President-elect Fakhrul
item.description:
Opposition Leader and Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami Ameer Dr Shafiqur Rahman has congratulated BNP candidate Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on his election as Bangladesh’s 23rd president.
Mirza Fakhrul secured 255 votes in Thursday’s presidential election.
In a Facebook post after the results were announced, Shafiqur congratulated the newly elected president and expressed hope that he would uphold justice, strengthen democracy, and protect the country’s independence and sovereignty.
“Today, August 20, 2026, the election for Bangladesh’s 23rd president was held. I extend my heartfelt congratulations to Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on being elected the 23rd president,” he said.
The Jamaat chief also expressed hope that Fakhrul would use his “utmost ability and wisdom” in discharging his responsibilities as head of state.
“I wish the newly elected President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir good health and longevity,” Shafiqur said.

item.title: Mirza Fakhrul: From student activist to Bangabhaban
item.description:
BNP candidate Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir has been elected Bangladesh’s 23rd president, capping a political journey that began with student activism at the University of Dhaka in the 1960s.
Fakhrul secured 255 votes in Thursday’s presidential election, defeating Jamaat-e-Islami-led 11-party alliance candidate Col (retd) Oli Ahmed, who received 88 votes. He won by a margin of 167 votes.
He is the first president to win a contested presidential election in 35 years.
From student activism to politics
Born on January 26, 1948, in Thakurgaon, Fakhrul earned bachelor’s and master’s degrees in economics from the University of Dhaka.
His political career began as a university student in the 1960s. He joined the East Pakistan Students Union (EPSU), the student wing of the East Pakistan Communist Party.
He later became general secretary of the organization’s SM Hall unit and eventually rose to become president of its Dhaka University unit in 1969, during the mass uprising against then-President Ayub Khan.
He was arrested and imprisoned for his political activities.
From teaching to government service
After completing his studies, Fakhrul began his professional career in 1972 as a lecturer at Dhaka College under the Bangladesh Civil Service’s education cadre.
He subsequently taught at several government colleges and also served as deputy director at the Directorate of Inspection and Audit. He later worked with the Bangladesh National Commission for UNESCO.
In late 1979, he joined late president Ziaur Rahman’s administration as private secretary to then-deputy prime minister SA Bari. He remained in the position until Bari resigned in 1982.
Fakhrul resigned from government service in 1986 and entered active politics.
In 1988, he was elected chairman of Thakurgaon municipality as an independent candidate.
He joined the BNP during the anti-Ershad movement in the early 1990s and was appointed president of the party’s Thakurgaon district unit in 1992.
Rise through the BNP
Fakhrul was elected to parliament from Thakurgaon-1 as a BNP candidate in the 2001 parliamentary election.
From 2001 to 2006, he served as state minister for agriculture and later as state minister for civil aviation and tourism.
He contested the 2008 parliamentary election but was defeated.
His rise within the BNP continued after the party’s fifth national council on December 8, 2009, when he was appointed senior joint secretary general.
He became the party’s acting secretary general on March 20, 2011, and held the position for five years.
On March 30, 2016, he was appointed BNP secretary general, becoming one of the party’s most prominent leaders.
He remained in the position until his election as president.
Family and political background
Fakhrul is married to Rahat Ara Begum, who studied at the University of Calcutta and works for an insurance company in Dhaka. They have two daughters, Mirza Shamaruh and Mirza Safaruh.
Shamaruh studied at the University of Dhaka and later joined the university as a teacher. She is currently a postdoctoral fellow in Australia.
Safaruh, who also studied at the University of Dhaka, teaches at a school in Dhaka.
Fakhrul’s younger brother, Mirza Faisal Amin, is president of the Thakurgaon district BNP and has also served as mayor of Thakurgaon municipality.
His father, Mirza Ruhul Amin, was a lawyer and politician who was elected to parliament several times from Thakurgaon and served as agriculture minister.
His uncle Mirza Ghulam Hafiz was a BNP politician who served as land minister, law, justice and parliamentary affairs minister, and speaker of the second parliament.
Another uncle, Wing Commander SR Mirza, served in the Mujibnagar government-in-exile during the Liberation War. He headed the Directorate of Youth Camps, which oversaw training facilities for freedom fighters.
From a student activist at Dhaka University to the secretary general of the BNP, and now the country’s president, Fakhrul’s political career spans more than five decades.

item.title: Five morning habits to keep your skin glowing
item.description:
Maintaining healthy, glowing skin requires consistent care, and morning can be an ideal time to establish a simple skincare routine. A few easy habits after waking up can help you start the day feeling fresh while supporting your skin's overall health.
Oil, sweat, and impurities can build up on the skin overnight. Start your morning by washing your face with a gentle cleanser suited to your skin type. After cleansing, apply a facial serum or a lightweight moisturizer to help keep the skin hydrated throughout the day.
Drinking enough fluids in the morning can help maintain hydration. Some people also prefer starting their day with a glass of lukewarm water with lemon. Lemons contain vitamin C and antioxidants, which are important nutrients for overall health and skin function. However, lemon water should not be considered a detox treatment or a substitute for a balanced diet.
You do not need an intense workout to get moving in the morning. A few minutes of stretching, simple freehand exercises, or a brisk walk around the garden or rooftop can be a good way to start the day. Regular physical activity supports overall health and circulation. Exercise can also give the skin a temporary post-workout glow as blood flow increases.
The moisturizer you use should suit your skin type. If your skin feels excessively tight after application or becomes unusually oily, the product may not be the right choice for you. During the daytime, using a moisturizer or skincare product with SPF can provide some protection from sunlight. For adequate sun protection, however, dermatologists generally recommend using a dedicated broad-spectrum sunscreen.
A balanced diet rich in fruits and vegetables can support healthy skin. Try adding fresh fruit or vegetables to your breakfast. Whole fruits are generally a better option than fruit juice because they provide fiber along with nutrients. Vegetables can also be included in meals or blended into smoothies. Rather than relying on any single food or drink for glowing skin, maintaining a balanced diet and staying hydrated can provide longer-term benefits.
Healthy-looking skin does not necessarily require an elaborate morning routine. Cleansing gently, moisturizing, protecting the skin from sunlight, staying hydrated, eating a balanced diet, and remaining physically active can all contribute to overall skin health. The key is consistency rather than following a long list of complicated skincare steps.

item.title: A New Era of Refrigerator Condenser Technology
Australian visa fraud: Nobody seems to care…
item.description:
Having been directly involved with the immigration law profession in Sydney for over 17 years, I have witnessed a harsh reality up close: when people are captivated by the sweet words of a fraudster, they perceive the truth-teller as an enemy.

While sitting in Sydney, I often receive calls or messages from both known and unknown persons from the country. Some relatives are coming to Australia on an apple or orange orchard picking visa, while others are lured by the promise of assured permanent residency in exchange for a significant amount of money.

When I scrutinise the documents and say, ‘This is sheer fraud; don’t give any money, ’ most people don’t want to believe it. Instead, they argue, ‘The visa is showing online!’ Some even say, ‘Since I am spending so much money, let’s see what happens!’ However, the inevitable happens; when the person loses all life savings and property and gets stranded at the airport or on foreign soil, another call comes. But by then, there’s nothing left to do.

Australia's immigration system is one of the most stringent and regulated frameworks worldwide. You cannot buy an Australian visa with money. The sole authority to grant visas lies with the Immigration Department of the country’s Ministry of Home Affairs. No individual, employer, agent, or even lawyer can guarantee a visa. If someone gives a ‘guarantee,’ understand that it's a scam. Unlike the Middle East, there’s no system of sponsorship or visa trade in Australia. Only if suitable local workers aren’t found can an Australian employer apply to recruit or sponsor a worker from abroad. This is a highly costly and lengthy process; very few people from Bangladesh can come through this route.

Australia’s immigration monitoring authority, OMARA, has recently intensified their surveillance manifold. Since 2021-22, disciplinary actions have been taken against more than 61 registered immigration consultants.

In Australia itself, licenses of several immigration consultants have been canceled for allegedly hiring unregistered fake brokers with their licenses. While such a clampdown on fraud is underway in Australia itself, the story of ‘assured visa’ spun for millions of taka while sitting in Bangladesh is so hollow and deceitful that one doesn’t need to be an expert to understand.

Recognising the fraudsters’ techniques and traps:

It is essential to recognise fraudsters' common tactics right from the start. The official website address of the Australian government ends with .gov. au. Fraudsters create fake websites with similar names ending in .com or .net and show false ‘visa verification’ setups there. They replicate letterheads and logos of reputed companies to create fake job offer letters. Calls made from internet numbers are used to convince you that they are coming directly from Australia. Their biggest bait is ‘Visa first, money later.

Fraud rings usually choose categories like Australia’s ‘Working Holiday’ (Subclass 417) or ‘e-Visitor’ (Subclass 651) visas, where Bangladesh isn’t even on the approved country list. Fraudsters quickly generate digital visas by inserting the name of an approved country in online application fields.

Then, using clever data amendments, they insert the applicant’s Bangladeshi passport number. Hence, even though the government’s primary verification system shows the visa as approved, traveling directly with that visa becomes impossible. Sometimes, they resort to ‘Maritime Crew’ (Subclass 988) visas. Victims are then initially sent to countries like Nepal, the Maldives, Fiji, or Indonesia, where Bangladeshis typically don’t need a visa. Remember, a proposal to detour via another country instead of buying a direct ticket from Dhaka to Australia is a significant sign of danger.

Warning from expat relatives also ignored:

Botany resident Tabarak Khan from Sydney shared his experience for a news report, saying, ‘My nephew fell into an agency’s trap. Although the visa showed up on government verification, I was certain it was fake just by seeing the type. I told him several times, there’s no shortcut. But he was so blinded by the fraudsters’ words that he didn’t listen to us. At the last moment, the entire fraud was exposed when he was buying a ticket to Nepal.’

Prominent businessman Harun Ur Rashid of Leppington, Sydney, also shared a similar experience. A ring made a deal of about Tk 1. 6 million with one of his relatives, luring him for permanent residency in three years on an agricultural visa. Harun Rashid said, ‘My relative didn’t even have the minimum English or professional qualification for a simple work visa. I had warned them in advance, but they didn’t listen. Later, when they tried to match the application and approval numbers, clear fraud was detected. ’

Many other expatriate Bangladeshis in Sydney have shared similar experiences. Enticed by flashy advertisements, people forget the fundamental rules and disregard realistic advice from relatives.

Practical lessons for protection from fraud:

1. A visa is impossible without language and professional assessment: For almost every work visa, a specified score in international English language tests (e. g. , IELTS) and a qualification certificate from an authorised organization are mandatory. Claims like ‘no English needed, no experience required’ mean definite fraud.

2. Consultations only with registered lawyers: According to Australian law, an immigration consultant must be registered with OMARA to provide visa consultation. Anyone can verify the name or licence number of any registered immigration consultant for free by visiting the official website (mara. gov. au).

3. Technology and verification: All Australian immigration work is conducted on the government’s only official portal (homeaffairs.gov.au). Thanks to today’s artificial intelligence and translation technology, anyone can easily convert and read English website information in Bengali. If necessary, it’s possible to speak with a government number or verify authenticity from the embassy.

4. Stop advance monetary transactions: Refrain from sending money to personal bank or mobile accounts and avoid health checkups outside the clinics designated by the Australian High Commission in Dhaka.

Dreaming of a bright future in Australia is not a crime, but due to lack of awareness and blind fascination, that dream shouldn’t turn into a disastrous nightmare. Legal qualifications and systematic pathways are the only keys to immigration. Many families can be saved from destitution by listening to warnings from relatives and experts in time.

#Kawsar Khan is Prothom Alo's Sydney correspondent and immigration lawyer.

*The opinions expressed here are the author’s own.

item.title: Foreign adviser: PM’s first India visit should be bilateral
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s first visit to India should be a bilateral visit rather than a meeting on the sidelines of multilateral platforms such as BRICS or the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), PM’s Foreign Affairs Adviser Humaiun Kobir said on Thursday.
“The first visit should be bilateral. We should invite each other to our homes, understand?” he said, describing Bangladesh and India as two important countries.
Talking to private TV channels at his office, Adviser Kobir said any visit should have a clear outcome, with mutual respect and engagement in place.
“There are issues related to the interests of the two countries, and these are not something to rush into,” he said. “When we see that the timing is right, we are willing to visit.”
He said groundwork needs to be done on several issues before the two sides can reach a consensus.
The adviser said that in recent days, Bangladesh has seen a fairly positive conversation from India, along with a strong realisation on the Indian side that the events of August 5 have deeply affected the sentiments of the people of Bangladesh.
“If India truly means resetting relations, then it must realise today’s Bangladesh,” Kobir said, noting that “in today’s Bangladesh, a terrorist like Sheikh Hasina or her party does not exist.”
“So, by recognizing this reality, we have to take the relationship forward,” the adviser said.
India’s promise to give the Prime Minister Tarique Rahman an “honourable welcome” during his visit makes New Delhi’s intent unmistakably clear, Indian media The Print reports, noting that the ball is now in Dhaka’s court.
Acknowledging that there are issues between the two neighbours, Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi on Tuesday night called on Bangladesh and India to move beyond their differences and work together to build a relationship based on “mutual and unconditional trust,” saying such differences can be resolved through engagement and dialogue.
“I can tell you I fully understand there are issues, but these issues can definitely be sorted out once the Prime Minister of Bangladesh (Tarique Rahman) and our Prime Minister Narendra Modi meet,” he said.
The Indian envoy also conveyed what he described as an assurance from Prime Minister Narendra Modi regarding a future visit by the Bangladesh prime minister to India.
“After meeting the prime minister here, I went straight to Delhi and had a great meeting with our prime minister. He (PM Modi) just mentioned one thing: we need to meet,” he said.
“You can tell them on my behalf that you have the prime minister of India’s assurance that when the prime minister of Bangladesh visits India, he will have such an honourable reception as he deserves,” he added, quoting the Indian prime minister.
The visit, Trivedi said, would be “a memorable visit” whose benefits would ultimately reach people and businesses on both sides.
On Sunday, Bangladesh urged India to act expeditiously on its request and help create a “propitious environment” for Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to make a bilateral visit to India.
"We are of the view that a propitious environment needs to be created for the visit," said AKM Shahidul Karim, spokesperson at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Officials of Bangladesh and India have been in touch with each other for several weeks on the possibility of a bilateral visit by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to India.
However, spokesperson Karim said this process was “vitiated” by the open press interaction in New Delhi on 5th August by Sheikh Hasina, who has been convicted by the International Crimes Tribunal for committing crimes against humanity.
"We have made our position clear on this matter," he said while reading out a written statement. The spokesperson, however, did not take any questions.
To this end, Bangladesh requested the Indian authorities to expeditiously act on its request to extradite Sheikh Hasina and other fugitive criminals, and to hand over to Bangladesh the accused killers of Shaheed Sharif Osman Hadi in compliance with their bilateral extradition treaty.
"We are awaiting their response," said the spokesperson.
Bangladesh reiterated that it will continue to pursue its "Bangladesh First" policy to promote friendly bilateral relations with other countries, including their neighbours, on the basis of sovereign equality, national dignity, non-interference in each other's internal affairs and mutual benefit.
On Hasina’s extradition request, the Indian government has recently said that the matter is being examined as part of ongoing judicial and internal legal processes.
Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) Spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal told reporters in New Delhi on Friday evening that they have extended an invitation to the prime minister of Bangladesh for a bilateral visit.
“We've also extended an invitation to the prime minister of Bangladesh for a visit to India for the outreach session of the BRICS Summit. So, these invitations have been extended, and I shall keep you updated if there is any progress in this regard,” he added.

DU female students reject curfew relaxation, demand complete repeal
item.description:
A group of female students at Dhaka University under the banner of Oborodhbashini has rejected a recommendation by the Provost Standing Committee to relax the “curfew” imposed on women’s dormitories, demanding its complete repeal instead.
At a press conference in front of Rokeya Hall on Thursday afternoon, the students said ensuring the safety of female students is the university administration’s responsibility and that restricting their movement in the name of security cannot be a solution.
Earlier on Monday, following a meeting of the Provost Standing Committee on Sunday, its Member Secretary and University Proctor Israt Ratan told Dhaka Tribune that the committee had recommended extending the deadline for female students to enter their halls by one hour. The recommendation is awaiting approval from the Syndicate.
The students have been protesting under the Oborodhbashini banner since July 30, demanding the withdrawal of the “evening curfew” in women’s halls and unrestricted movement around the clock.
As part of their campaign, they have distributed leaflets and posters in women’s dormitories, organised marches and sit-ins in academic areas, and collected mass signatures from female students.
Their three-point demands include the immediate abolition of the existing “discriminatory evening curfew” currently in effect from 10pm to 6am while ensuring adequate security and unrestricted movement for female students around the clock.
They also demand that female students be allowed to enter any women’s hall by showing valid identification and stay overnight with proper permission, as well as ensuring access to all female relatives of women students.
At the press conference, Israt Jahan Emu, a student of Shamsun Nahar Hall, said more than 1,200 female students signed a memorandum submitted to the vice-chancellor on August 9.
She said a solidarity rally on August 10 also issued an ultimatum to the administration to repeal the evening curfew. However, instead of addressing their demands, the administration proposed only a one-hour relaxation of the curfew, she alleged.
The students said the proposal undermines the civil and fundamental rights of female students and stressed that there is no scope for compromise on the issue.

Simmons urges Bangladesh to stay grounded
item.description:
Bangladesh coach Phil Simmons has urged his players to keep their emotions under control and maintain the discipline that produced a historic Test victory over Australia as they prepare for the second and final Test in Mackay.
Bangladesh stunned Australia by nine wickets in Darwin last week to secure their first Test victory on Australian soil. They now have an opportunity to claim their first Test series win in the southern hemisphere, but Simmons knows the hosts are likely to respond strongly at Harrup Park from Saturday.
Simmons described the Darwin triumph as the best Test victory of his coaching career, which has included stints with Ireland, Zimbabwe, the West Indies and Afghanistan.
“I've had other formats with big ones but, in Tests, it is the best,” Simmons said after Thursday’s training session.
The 63-year-old Trinidadian, who scored a Test century at the Melbourne Cricket Ground during his playing career, stressed that Australia would return with greater intensity in Mackay.
“The only thing I had to say to them is that Australia is going to come harder. So we have to either keep that level of performance or get a little bit better,” he said.
Simmons had already warned his players against becoming carried away by their landmark victory. In the dressing room after the Darwin Test, he reminded them that their achievement would remain one of the biggest moments of their careers, while also insisting that the series was only halfway through.
The coach admitted that controlling emotions could be particularly challenging for his Bangladesh players after such a significant result.
“Bangladesh people are emotional – and I am not the same,” Simmons said with a smile. “So it's easy for me to control that, but it's difficult for them.”
However, he was encouraged by what he saw at training, saying the players appeared to have settled after several days to absorb the significance of their victory.
Simmons could also have another pace option at his disposal with Shoriful Islam pushing for a return to the XI. The left-arm quick missed the first Test with a side strain but bowled an impressive spell in the nets on Thursday and appears to have recovered fully.
Shoriful offers Bangladesh an additional dimension with his pace, height and left-arm angle. He also took six wickets against Australia in an ODI in June.
Simmons, however, remains reluctant to alter a winning combination, with Taijul Islam and Ebadot Hossain among those who could potentially make way if Shoriful is selected.
“He offers something different, but again, we just won a Test match, so I am one who hardly likes to change winning XIs,” Simmons said.
Bangladesh did receive some injury concerns during training. Opener Tanzid Hasan, who scored his maiden Test century in Darwin, did not bat because of a neck issue. Mushfiqur Rahim was struck on a finger while batting in the nets but returned to training and is expected to be available for the second Test.
Simmons was particularly pleased with Bangladesh’s bowling effort in Darwin, where their attack repeatedly kept Australia’s batters under pressure through disciplined lines and lengths.
He said the same approach would be required in Mackay against an Australian batting order capable of responding quickly.
“They are good batsmen, they're world-class batsmen,” Simmons said. “As long as we stick to what we've planned and make sure that they're under pressure all the time, that's what we ask for.”
With history within reach, Bangladesh will need to reproduce the composure and consistency that carried them to their remarkable Darwin victory.

Mismanagement, overcrowding plague RMCH
item.description:
Patients at Rangpur Medical College Hospital (RMCH) are facing severe sanitation problems, overcrowding and complaints over the availability of medicines and healthcare services.
A visit to several wards, including the medicine, gynaecology and paediatric departments, found dirty water overflowing from toilets, piles of waste and leftover food, and a persistent foul smell.
In the male medicine ward, wastewater from a toilet had reportedly spread across the floor and reached areas where patients were staying. Patients and their attendants were seen covering their noses while moving through the ward.
Rahman, who came from Bhurungamari in Kurigram with his father, said they had been staying in the ward for three days without a bed and were forced to sleep on the floor.
“The foul-smelling wastewater from the toilet has reached our sleeping area. We are somehow managing to stay here,” he said.
He also alleged that the toilet door latch was broken, making it difficult to use the facility. According to him, around 150 patients in the ward have access to only one toilet.
Mamina Begum, from Saidpur in Nilphamari, said her husband was admitted to a paying bed, but they were also facing problems caused by wastewater and poor sanitation around the toilet.
“How can anyone stay in such an environment?” she questioned.
She also alleged that doctors often visit only once or twice a day and that patients are frequently asked to undergo diagnostic tests outside the hospital.
Another patient, Mamtaz Mia of Badarganj in Rangpur, alleged that patients have to purchase most medicines from outside.
“Except for a few tablets, we have to buy almost everything from outside,” he said.
The hospital has an official capacity of 1,000 beds, but hospital staff said more than 2,500 patients stay there on an average day.
As a result, many patients are being treated on floors, in corridors and on verandas, further worsening sanitation and putting additional pressure on hospital facilities.
Nurses and attendants said the excessive patient load has contributed to the problems, while patients and their relatives complained about inadequate cleaning and maintenance.
Several toilets in different wards were reportedly found in poor condition. Leftover food and other waste were also seen around toilet areas, contributing to the foul smell.
Patients and attendants also complained about stray dogs roaming freely inside the hospital building.
They said dogs could be seen on different floors, raising concerns about hygiene and patient safety.
Patients also alleged that essential medicines are often unavailable at the hospital and that they are forced to buy them from outside pharmacies.
Some patients further alleged that a broker syndicate operates inside the hospital and claimed that unscrupulous employees are involved in the network.
They called for stronger monitoring and surprise inspections by senior authorities to ensure that the actual condition of the hospital is properly assessed.
When contacted, Rangpur Medical College Hospital Director Brigadier General Ashikur Rahman said he had been informed about the allegations regarding sanitation, overflowing wastewater, toilet facilities, overcrowding and the availability of medicines.
He assured that the issues would be taken seriously and that steps would be taken to address them.
The hospital, one of the major public healthcare facilities in northern Bangladesh, is under significant pressure due to the large number of patients it serves.
Patients and their relatives are now calling for urgent measures to improve sanitation, repair toilets, ensure adequate supplies of medicines and strengthen overall hospital management.

item.title: Historic ballot sends Mirza Fakhrul to Bangabhaban
item.description:
Bangladesh elected its president through a parliamentary vote for the first time in nearly 35 years on Thursday, with BNP candidate Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir defeating opposition contender Col (retd) Oli Ahmad by a commanding 255-88 margin to become the country’s 23rd president.
The election ended more than three decades of uncontested presidential races and marked another major turn in Fakhrul’s political career after around 15 years at the helm of the BNP as its secretary general.
Chief Election Commissioner AMM Nasir Uddin, who served as returning officer, announced the result after voting ended at 5pm at the National Parliament.
“Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir has secured 255 votes. I declare that, having received the highest number of votes, he has been duly elected president,” Nasir Uddin announced.
The Election Commission subsequently issued a gazette notification formally declaring Fakhrul president.
Of 349 eligible lawmakers, 343 cast their votes. Fakhrul received 255 votes, while Oli, the candidate of the Jamaat-e-Islami-led 11-party opposition alliance, secured 88.
Six lawmakers did not vote — BNP MPs Mirza Abbas, Mostafa Kamal Pasha and Dr Muhammad Osman Faruk; independent MP Rumeen Farhana; Jamaat MP Gazi Nazrul Islam; and Islami Andolan Bangladesh MP Md Oli Ullah.
The announcement triggered celebrations inside the Parliament Chamber, with lawmakers thumping their desks as Fakhrul raised his hand to acknowledge their congratulations.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman presented the president-elect with a red rose before shaking hands and embracing him.
In a notable display of political cordiality after the contest, Leader of the Opposition Dr Shafiqur Rahman and Deputy Leader of the Opposition Syed Abdullah Mohammed Taher approached the treasury bench with other opposition lawmakers.
Fakhrul left his seat and embraced Shafiqur.
Tarique then embraced Fakhrul, while the prime minister and opposition leader also exchanged an embrace.
Lawmakers from the treasury and opposition benches subsequently exchanged greetings as the chamber took on a celebratory atmosphere.
Fakhrul later shook hands with CEC Nasir Uddin and greeted election officials.
Bangabhaban is preparing to hold the oath-taking ceremony for the new president on Friday evening.
Voting took place from 2pm to 5pm through an open ballot.
Acting President Hafiz Uddin Ahmad and acting Speaker Barrister Kayser Kamal cast their votes at 2:10pm, followed a minute later by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and Fakhrul.
With the Chittagong-4 seat vacant, 349 lawmakers were eligible to vote.
The National Parliament currently has 247 BNP MPs, 77 from Jamaat, eight from NCP, eight independents, three from Bangladesh Khilafat Majlis, and one each from Bangladesh Jatiya Party-BJP, Gono Odhikar Parishad, Ganosamhati Andolon, Khilafat Majlis, Islami Andolan Bangladesh and Jatiya Ganatantrik Party.
The BNP-led ruling camp commands 250 seats, while the 11-party opposition alliance has 90.
The result nevertheless showed Fakhrul receiving five votes more than the ruling camp’s stated strength, while Oli received two fewer than the opposition alliance’s 90 seats.
With six lawmakers absent, the open-ballot result provides an unusual glimpse of votes crossing the formal political divide.
The previous contested presidential election was held on October 8, 1991, when BNP candidate Abdur Rahman Biswas defeated Awami League candidate Badrul Haider Chowdhury by 172 votes to 92.
Every presidential election since then had ended without a ballot because only one candidate remained in contention.
Thursday’s election was triggered by Mohammed Shahabuddin’s resignation on July 24, after which Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad assumed responsibility as acting president.
Under Article 123(2) of the Constitution, an election must be held within 90 days when the presidency falls vacant following a resignation.

item.title: Congratulations pour in for Fakhrul
item.description:
Congratulations poured in from political leaders, foreign missions and prominent figures on Thursday evening after Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir was elected Bangladesh’s 23rd president, with messages expressing hopes that the veteran politician would uphold democracy, justice and the dignity of the country’s highest constitutional office.
Nobel laureate Professor Muhammad Yunus, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, Opposition Leader Dr Shafiqur Rahman and Fakhrul’s presidential rival Col (retd) Oli Ahmad were among those congratulating him, while China and the United Kingdom were among the first foreign partners to publicly welcome his election.
Fakhrul defeated Oli, the candidate of the Jamaat-e-Islami-led 11-party opposition alliance, by 255 votes to 88 in Thursday’s presidential election, the first contested race for Bangabhaban in nearly 35 years.
The Election Commission subsequently issued a gazette declaring him elected president.
Professor Yunus extended his “heartfelt congratulations and best wishes” to Fakhrul, describing his political career of more than five decades as closely intertwined with Bangladesh’s political history.
He said: “His organizational skills, wisdom, leadership during times of crisis, and extensive experience working closely with people at the grassroots level have established him as a distinctive figure in the country’s national politics.”
Yunus expressed confidence that Fakhrul’s background as an academic, seasoned politician and “man of principle” would help him further uphold the dignity of the presidency.
He said: “I look forward to Bangladesh advancing towards greater prosperity, justice, and democracy under the leadership of President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir. I wish his excellency good health, a long life, and every success in the discharge of his responsibilities.”
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman was among the first to congratulate Fakhrul immediately after the result was announced inside the National Parliament.
Tarique shook hands with Fakhrul, presented him with a red rose and later embraced him as lawmakers thumped their desks in congratulations.
The celebrations also produced a display of political cordiality across the aisle, with opposition leaders approaching the treasury bench after the result.
Opposition Leader and Jamaat Ameer Dr Shafiqur Rahman congratulated Fakhrul and expressed hope that he would use his “utmost ability and wisdom” to uphold justice and democracy and protect Bangladesh’s independence and sovereignty.
“I extend my heartfelt congratulations to Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on being elected the 23rd president,” Shafiqur said in a Facebook post.
Col (retd) Oli Ahmad also congratulated Fakhrul after losing the presidential contest.
In a message, the LDP chairman expressed hope that Fakhrul would uphold the Constitution and discharge his responsibilities with firmness and competence while safeguarding independence, democracy and justice.
Oli also wished him good health and a long life.
The gesture came after a rare competitive presidential election. Bangladesh had not witnessed a contested vote for the presidency since 1991.
Foreign congratulations also began arriving shortly after Fakhrul’s victory.
The Chinese Embassy in Dhaka said: “Warm congratulations to Mirza Fakharul Islam Alamgir on his election as president of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh.”
China said it attached great importance to its relationship with Bangladesh and was ready to work closely with Dhaka to deepen bilateral cooperation and deliver greater benefits to the peoples of both countries.
The British High Commission also congratulated Fakhrul, signalling its intention to work with the new head of state.
It said: “The UK looks forward to working with Hon. President Fakhrul and the Government of Bangladesh to further strengthen the close and longstanding partnership between our two countries.”
As of Thursday evening, searches of current published reports found these as the principal publicly reported congratulations; additional messages from foreign governments and political leaders may follow after Fakhrul formally takes office.
The 78-year-old veteran politician is expected to be sworn in on Friday evening, completing his transition from longtime BNP secretary general and Cabinet minister to Bangabhaban.

item.title: 22 years on, August 21 wounds remain, justice question returns
item.description:
Twenty-two years after grenades rained down on an Awami League rally at Bangabandhu Avenue, survivors of one of Bangladesh’s deadliest political attacks are marking another August 21 with the physical and psychological scars still intact, but with the legal case ending in the acquittal of all those convicted by the trial court.
The August 21, 2004 attack killed 24 people and injured more than 100 as grenades exploded at a rally addressed by then opposition leader Sheikh Hasina.
More than two decades later, survivors say their struggle has moved beyond the injuries they suffered that afternoon to questions of justice, financial hardship and, for some, a new life of insecurity.
For Md Anwar Parvez Tinku, an eyewitness and injured survivor, the memories remain vivid.
Recalling the moments before the attack, he said Sheikh Hasina had climbed onto a truck to address the rally, surrounded by senior Awami League leaders, when the explosions began.
He said: “Apa was going to give a speech on the microphone, at that moment grenades started exploding like rain. We scattered like flower petals everywhere. Leaders and activists formed a human shield to save Apa. Blood flowed all around, heads, hands and feet of many present were scattered around. It felt like my right leg had been blown off.”
Twenty-two years later, Tinku said the trauma still follows him into his sleep.
He said: “After the grenade attack, the police there did not take us to the hospital either. They fired tear gas. I was severely injured in the grenade attack on my right leg.”
Doctors at several hospitals recommended amputating his leg, he said, before another physician managed to save it through surgery. But the injuries continue to affect his life.
“I am suffering from leg pain, and besides, I have a bomb scar on my body. I cannot do any work. I am somehow surviving with a daughter and a wife. My brothers pay some expenses every month, so I go on. Due to lack of money, I cannot even get my leg treated,” he said.
The anniversary comes against a dramatically changed legal backdrop.
In October 2018, Dhaka’s Speedy Trial Tribunal-1 sentenced 19 people, including former state minister for home affairs Lutfuzzaman Babar and former deputy minister Abdus Salam Pintu, to death.
Another 19, including Tarique Rahman, were sentenced to life imprisonment, while 11 others received varying prison terms.
But the convictions were subsequently overturned.
The High Court acquitted all those convicted in the cases, and on September 4, 2025, a six-member Appellate Division bench unanimously dismissed the state’s appeal, leaving the acquittals intact.
The legal reversal has left survivors such as Tinku questioning whether they will ever see anyone held responsible.
He said: “Many of our comrades have been killed and injured. The murder of those who were killed has not been tried yet. I want to see the trial of those who ordered, financed and planned the grenade attack before they die. This will give peace to the souls of our fallen comrades.”
For some survivors, the political upheaval following the fall of the Awami League government in August 2024 has brought another layer of hardship.
Several victims, who wished to remain anonymous due to safety concerns, told Dhaka Tribune that they had subsequently been implicated in criminal cases, while some had gone into hiding.
They alleged their homes had been attacked or burned and their families were struggling financially.
Some said they were working anonymously as rickshaw pullers or labourers to survive.
One woman injured in the grenade attack described the desperation of living with both the old wounds and her present circumstances.
She said: “I have come back from the door of death. However, it was better to die. It is difficult to survive the lawsuit and police harassment. I have no money to eat, how can I file a case?”
Some survivors are also critical of the former Awami League government, saying it had years in power to ensure a definitive judicial conclusion to the attack.
They said the injured were repeatedly brought before television cameras around August 21, but their suffering became entangled with partisan politics rather than producing lasting closure.
The attack itself has passed into Bangladesh’s political history.
Its judicial journey has travelled from investigation and trial to mass convictions, appeals and ultimately the acquittal of all those convicted.
Yet for those who were standing on Bangabandhu Avenue 22 years ago, August 21 is not merely history.
The court cases may have reached their legal conclusion, but survivors still carry grenade splinters, disabilities and memories of the dead.
For them, another anniversary arrives with the most fundamental question still unsettled: who will ultimately be held accountable for August 21?

item.title: ‘Investors can’t underwrite a company in a market they can’t picture’
item.description:
Hussain Elius, co-founder of Pathao, speaks to Dhaka Tribune’s Wafiur Rahman about life after Pathao, the structural problems holding back Bangladesh’s startup ecosystem, lessons from building one of the country’s biggest tech companies, and the void left by his friend and early backer Fahim Saleh.
Since Pathao, I started Wind, a cross-border payments company built on blockchain rails. The pitch is simple: move money across borders faster, cheaper and more transparently than the correspondent banking system, which typically charges 3% to 5% and settles slowly. The company was acquired by Fin.com in the US in 2024.
The difference from Pathao wasn’t just the product; it was the entire operating mode. Pathao was a street fight: riders, red helmets, no rulebook, building trust with a population that had never split a fare with an app before.
Wind is quieter and more technical. There are no drivers to onboard or traffic police to negotiate with. Instead, there are compliance regimes, banking partners and licensing conversations, because this time we’re moving other people’s money, not just their packages.
I also recently released Moving Bangladesh: The Origin Story of Pathao, a business book and biography about how we built the company. It is the unfiltered, tactical reality of scaling Pathao, not the version that ends up in press releases, and the lessons we learned from building one of Bangladesh’s largest tech companies.
I’ll caveat this properly: I’ve been out of the operating seat since 2021, so take this as an informed outsider’s read, not an insider’s.
The opportunity is that the current funding winter is brutal for the ecosystem, but it’s arguably good news for the strongest incumbent in it.
When capital is scarce, weaker, capital-dependent competitors get forced into the open -- unpaid wages, shrinking headcounts, emergency requests to state funds.
Pathao has already survived its own near-death experience in 2019 and came out the other side disciplined about unit economics. It is structurally in a better position to consolidate market share while others are just trying to make payroll.
That’s a speculative read on my part, since I don’t have their internal numbers anymore, but it’s consistent with how these cycles usually play out.
The challenge is that the ceiling I wrote about in the book hasn’t moved. Bangladesh is roughly three cities’ worth of addressable ride and delivery demand.
Rapido in India expanded into a hundred cities and is now worth multiples of Pathao’s peak valuation, largely because India kept giving them a next city to enter.
Pathao’s fourth market was Nepal, not because it was the biggest opportunity, but because it was the only one left that made sense to reach without a bigger balance sheet.
Whatever Pathao does next -- fintech, deeper logistics infrastructure for the rest of the ecosystem, more of Nepal -- it has to solve the same problem I never fully solved: how do you build something Bangladesh-sized into something regionally or globally sized without the capital that usually funds that jump?
Yes, and it’s not the thing people usually guess. It wasn’t the spending, the hiring pace or even the layoffs. Those were mistakes too, but they were forced mistakes, made under real constraints.
The real one was this: when we had the cash and momentum to push into a genuinely large market, we expanded into a small one.
We went to Nepal instead of India.
At the time, it was the obviously sensible choice -- geographically close, culturally similar, and our playbook ported over almost unchanged.
That’s exactly what made it the wrong call.
By the time I understood what that decision cost us, cheap global capital had dried up. Grab and Gojek had Southeast Asia locked down, while Uber, Ola and Rapido had India locked down. We didn’t have the runway or the energy to fight a second war in someone else’s backyard.
If I’m being honest with myself, that single choice -- safe over ambitious, at the one moment we had the resources to be ambitious -- mattered more to Pathao’s ceiling than any operational decision we made in seven years.
The answer isn’t about talent or ideas. It’s about what happens after a startup runs out of money, or after it needs a real exit.
In deep-capital markets, a struggling company has options: a strategic buyer, a bridge round, sometimes even a public listing on growth metrics alone.
In Bangladesh, none of those exist at scale. The public market isn’t deep enough for a real tech IPO. There’s no meaningful base of strategic acquirers.
The local investor community is small and genuinely risk-averse, not irrationally so; they just don’t have the balance sheets to absorb frontier-market losses. And foreign capital shows up late, conditional on proof that a cash-burning company usually can’t produce yet.
I call this the “Bangladesh Tax”: every company here that depends on outside capital to survive pays it, one way or another.
There’s a second, less visible layer: the LP mandate problem.
Global venture capital doesn’t flow because a fund manager personally likes your pitch. It flows because a fund has a documented mandate -- geography, stage, sector -- that a pension fund or endowment board signed off on.
Bangladesh, for most of the last decade, simply wasn’t inside anyone’s mandate.
That’s not a judgment on the quality of the founders or ideas. It is a structural fact about how institutional capital gets allocated.
Every market that eventually gets a mandate -- Vietnam, Indonesia a decade ago -- started without one. Someone has to be the first deal that gives the next fund a comparable to point to when they go back to their own LPs.
I’d separate two things that are easy to conflate here: sentiment and mandate.
Sentiment has clearly gotten worse in the short term.
Chaldal was, by reputation, one of the most disciplined operators in the country, and its 2026 liquidity crisis -- unpaid wages, protests outside the Jessore facility, a Tk40 crore working-capital shortfall, an emergency request to Startup Bangladesh that reportedly fell through -- is being read by longtime sceptics as vindication that the whole “startup boom” narrative was overstated.
That reaction is happening in real time on social media and in the trade press, and it’s not helping anyone currently raising.
But the deeper issue, the mandate problem I mentioned earlier, was never really about perception, and I don’t think one company’s stress, however prominent, moves it much either way.
Bangladesh not being inside most global funds’ investable geography wasn’t a verdict on Chaldal, Pathao or ShopUp specifically. It was a structural fact before any of these companies existed.
My somewhat speculative read is that Chaldal’s troubles will sting locally and will be cited by critics for a while, but they’re unlikely to be the deciding factor in whether international capital allocators add Bangladesh to their mandates.
What actually moves that needle is a handful of clean, comparable exits, the kind that let a fund manager tell their own LPs: “This is a known, investable category now.”
We haven’t had enough of those yet.
A few things I wish someone had told me plainly when I started out.
First, understand the fundraising stack and don’t skip layers. Most advice jumps straight from “get an angel” to “raise a Series A” as if they sit next to each other. They don’t.
There’s a middle layer, expert individual capital without a fund’s formal structure: super angels, family offices, people who invest on conviction and relationships rather than a mandate. Know which layer you’re actually talking to, and pitch accordingly.
Second, a “no” is often about the fund’s mandate, not your company. Some of the sharpest investors I sat across from passed on Pathao, not because the analysis was weak, but because their fund’s structure genuinely couldn’t hold a frontier-market position on the timeline required.
Don’t over-update on a rejection without knowing which kind it was.
Third, sell the market before you sell the company if you’re outside the mapped geographies. I used to walk into rooms in Singapore and spend the first 20 minutes explaining why Bangladesh mattered before I ever got to Pathao.
That’s still true for most Bangladeshi founders today.
Investors can’t underwrite a company in a market they can’t picture.
Fourth, build the unit economics story before you build the growth story. The single best piece of advice I ignored came from a Russian investor who told me in 2018 to “be a cockroach, not a unicorn.”
Know your break-even volume for every product line before you launch the next one.
Investors trust a founder who’s choosing to grow faster with their capital far more than one who needs it to survive.
Finally, fundraise yourself. Don’t outsource it. Every time I’ve seen a founder hand fundraising to an external hire or a CFO, it’s gone badly.
No one can sell your company’s conviction the way you can, and no serious investor backs a company whose CEO isn’t personally the one asking.
Fahim was the first person who bet on me, before there was a “Bangladesh startup ecosystem” for anyone to bet on.
He said yes to sponsoring a joke website I made for $200 before he’d ever met me. That instinct, seeing a person rather than a market, isn’t something institutional capital is built to do.
Without him, I don’t know if I aim as high, as early, or if I ever end up in the rooms that eventually built Pathao.
What his death took from Bangladesh’s startup scene is harder to see from the outside, and I think it’s the part that gets missed.
Fahim wasn’t only backing Pathao. He was the person a handful of other founders called when a round wasn’t closing, when a key hire fell through, when someone needed a person who’d actually done it to tell them it was going to be okay.
When he died, that support beam went with him.
Some of those companies made it through anyway. Most didn’t.
The real cost isn’t just the companies he built; it’s the companies that never got the chance to start because the person who would have made the first, irrational, conviction-based bet on them wasn’t there anymore.
That’s a harder loss to put a number on than anything on a cap table.

Women’s safety or a new unwritten boundary?
item.description:
Reports of women being refused entry onto regular public buses, whether made in jest or whether such a practice is beginning to emerge, are not something to simply laugh off.
Every day, countless women in Dhaka travel by bus to offices, universities, schools, and for countless other reasons. For them, getting on a bus is never simply about travelling from one place to another. It involves the pressure of reaching somewhere on time, concerns about safety, the struggle to find a place in a crowded vehicle, and countless small and large discomforts that have become part of everyday life.
Consider the experience of one such woman a reflection of what many others go through. She takes public buses to work every day. One day, she raises her hand as a bus approaches. The bus stops. But as she tries to get on, she is told, “There are no seats.”
She replies, “That’s okay. I can stand.”
Yet the response is, “If we take you, we will have to take fewer male passengers.” Sometimes, even after getting on the bus, a male passenger sitting nearby may complain, “it becomes difficult to stand when women get on.” But that woman is a citizen of the same city. She too needs to reach her office at a particular time. She too needs to get home at the end of the day. And she may have no other alternative.
The question is simple: Why is a woman standing considered a problem when a man standing is treated as perfectly normal?
On Dhaka’s regular public buses, there are seats designated for women. But the reality is that these seats are often located beside the engine. Sitting there amid intense heat, noise, fumes, and discomfort can be physically difficult.
Yet women sit there because those are the seats “designated for women.” But when a woman chooses not to sit beside the engine and instead takes a relatively more comfortable seat, questions are raised: “Why are you sitting there? That is a men’s seat.”
Sometimes, it feels as though all the remaining seats on a bus are informally reserved for men, while the few designated seats for women constitute the entirety of a woman’s entitlement to public transportation.
This is where the conversation around pink buses becomes particularly important.
A separate bus service for women can, on the surface, certainly be a positive initiative. Safe, comfortable, and harassment-free transportation can make mobility easier for women. Many women may feel safer and more at ease travelling on such buses.
But an important question remains: In creating special facilities for women, is there a risk of unintentionally pushing them away from the public facilities they are equally entitled to use?
If pink buses are available, could women gradually be made to feel that boarding a regular bus is somehow “unusual”? Today, someone may jokingly say, “There are pink buses for women.” But what happens tomorrow if a bus worker actually starts believing that refusing a female passenger is somehow justified because a separate service exists?
Creating a separate arrangement for women must not, at the same time, shrink their rights on regular public transportation. A similar dynamic can already be observed in the case of women-only compartments on the metro rail.
Dedicated compartments have undoubtedly created an additional option for safety and comfort, and that is a positive development. But the problem arises when a woman cannot get into the designated compartment and chooses to board another one.
Sometimes, she may hear, “There is a women’s compartment.” But if a woman chooses to stand in another compartment because it is more convenient for her, is she actually breaking any rule?
Having a designated space and losing the right to use other spaces are not the same thing. Special facilities should not replace rights; they should make exercising those rights safer and easier.
That distinction is crucial. Safety, but not separation Why would a woman want a pink bus? Because she wants to get home without harassment. Because she wants to stand in a crowded bus without the fear of unwanted physical contact. Because she does not want to be refused entry simply because she is a woman. Because she wants the journey home at the end of a long workday to be a journey not another battle.
But that same woman also wants to be able to board a regular public bus as an ordinary passenger. She does not want her gender to determine the extent of her right to move around her own city.
Therefore, rather than questioning whether pink buses are necessary, the more important question is: Why has such a system become necessary in the first place? If the regular public transportation system is safe, respectful, and accessible to everyone regardless of gender, then a dedicated women’s bus can simply be an additional option.
But if women continue to face obstacles when boarding regular buses, standing inside them, or occupying seats, then pink buses do not solve the underlying problem. They merely provide an alternative route around it. A city should not reach a point where the solution to women’s safety is simply to separate women.
Ultimately, Dhaka needs a public transportation system where a woman does not have to wonder:
“Which bus will actually let me get on today?” Instead, she should be able to think:
“Whichever bus arrives, I can board it as a passenger.” Because safe mobility is not a privilege.
It is a basic civic right.
Samira Tasnim and ASM Rafad Asgar are Research Associates, Bangladesh Institute of Governance and Management (BIGM).

item.title: August 21: A legacy of unpunished terror
item.description:
Today, the world pays tribute to the victims and survivors of terrorism. We honour their courage, amplify their voices, and reaffirm the global community’s commitment to their dignity and rights.
Since 2017, the United Nations has observed August 21 as the “International Day of Remembrance of and Tribute to the Victims of Terrorism.”
Reading the UN secretary-general’s commemorative message reminds me of the 24 souls who lost their lives in the deadliest act of terrorism in my own country 22 years ago.
In Bangladesh’s history, August 21 is overwhelmingly defined by the 2004 grenade attack. It is considered the nation’s most devastating act of terrorism, occurring when military-grade hand grenades were detonated at an anti-terrorism rally organized by the Awami League on Bangabandhu Avenue in Dhaka.
Now-deposed former prime minister Sheikh Hasina, then the leader of the opposition, narrowly escaped death when party leaders formed a human shield around her. However, the barrage of blasts claimed 24 lives and, by some accounts, left more than 500 others injured, with injuries ranging from minor wounds to permanent disabilities.
With “Healing through Memory” serving as the theme for this year’s observance, I struggle to heal my own wounds as an ordinary member of society. Memory remains our only solace because nobody has been held legally accountable for this heinous offence.
Luckily, I was not on duty at Bangabandhu Avenue on that fateful day. However, during my years as a newspaper journalist, I was no stranger to witnessing terror -- much of which spiked around the turn of the century in the early 2000s. I vividly remember a close shave while covering a rally at the historic Paltan Maidan in early 2001.
A sudden bomb attack at a Communist Party of Bangladesh (CPB) rally caught everyone off guard. It was the afternoon of January 20. As the rally progressed, a loud explosion rang out, and I immediately saw at least three people collapse just feet from where I stood. Like everyone else, I ran for my life. Police and hospital reports later confirmed five deaths and more than three dozen injuries.
To this day, it brings some comfort that the state apparatus successfully investigated the CPB rally attack, hunting down the terror outfit and its operatives. Unfortunately, justice has completely eluded the victims of the much larger tragedy unleashed on August 21, 2004.
As the UN secretary-general aptly notes, this day reminds us that remembrance is a pathway to recovery and renewal. Yet, a critical question remains: how we remember matters.
In my view, true remembrance requires two things: Paying befitting homage to the 24 victims while consoling their families, and ensuring that the offenders are brought to justice. Tragically, we have failed on the second front.
The bare minimum we owe those 24 souls is a proper investigation, accurate identification of the criminals, and due punishment. After years of investigation, a special tribunal in 2018 sentenced 19 people to death and 19 others to life imprisonment.
However, following major political shifts in Bangladesh, the judicial trajectory changed drastically through multiple appeals. The initial convictions of top political figures and militants ultimately gave way to the complete exoneration of all the accused by the country’s highest court.
The High Court declared the original trial legally flawed, invalidating the charge sheets over procedural misconduct and a lack of credible evidence.
When the state challenged the decision, a seven-member bench of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on September 4, 2025, upholding the acquittals of all 38 accused.
Over the decades, the nation has watched investigations fall apart and witnessed staged dramas such as the infamous “Joj Mia” fabrication, which relied on false confessions extracted under duress.
Every year, political bodies observe this date as “Grenade Attack Day” to honour the dead. Yet, I wonder how they face the survivors and bereaved families when we have collectively failed as a nation to punish the perpetrators.
Ideally, a tragedy as massive as that of August 21 should have united a shocked nation. Instead, we remained fiercely loyal to our political divides, weaponizing competing narratives over who was responsible. Rather than standing united against terror, we allowed it to divide us.
This year marks the first time we are observing the International Day of Remembrance since the Supreme Court’s final acquittal late last year. It is up to jurists and legal experts to debate whether the state can still pursue fresh, impartial investigations or search for solid evidence. As ordinary citizens, however, we see only a national failure.
I echo the words of the UN secretary-general: “Today and every day, let us stand in solidarity with victims and survivors and build a future free from violence and fear.”
Reaz Ahmad is Editor, Dhaka Tribune.
